ewca/civ/2021/594.rationale:
Addison Lee v Lange [2021] EWCA Civ 594 is a leading Court of Appeal authority squarely on the question: it holds that minicab/e-hail app drivers are limb (b) workers under s.230(3)(b) ERA 1996, applying Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5 and Autoclenz, and consequently that they are entitled to NMW and holiday pay. The judgment also directly addresses the follow-on question of how working time (and hence the periods for which NMW and holiday pay must be paid) is to be identified — the "logged on" periods — upholding the ET's working time findings under the Working Time Regulations and distinguishing Slovenian Radio and Television. This is directly on-point, not merely useful background, so grade 3.

On the highlights: [0] states the ET's determination that the drivers were s.230(3)(b) workers — squarely supportive. [1] identifies the periods for which pay is due (time logged on), which is the practical crux of the minimum wage/holiday pay entitlement — supportive. [2] merely records the parties' competing submissions on whether the working time definition is a "workable" route to holiday pay/NMW questions; it frames the dispute without supplying any reasoning or answer, so it does not itself help answer the question.

ewca/civ/2018/2748.rationale:
Uber BV v Aslam [2018] EWCA Civ 2748 is the leading Court of Appeal authority, and indeed the leading UK authority, on whether ride-hailing (Uber) drivers are workers entitled to national minimum wage and holiday pay. The court (Mcullen LJ, Bean LJ concurring; Lady Justice Rose dissenting on the WTR issue) held that the drivers were workers for s.230(3) ERA 1996, confirming the ET's approach of looking at the reality of the relationship rather than the contractual labels, and remitted the NMWR issues (including whether waiting time is "work" and whether there are restrictions on other work) to the employment tribunal. It is directly on point for the question asked and would be the first authority cited by any lawyer. The matched paragraphs (12, 15, 16, 34) set out the factual and contractual context and the Autoclenz/Secret Hotels2 reasoning on statutory purpose, which is directly relevant.

Highlight assessment:
[0] Directly relevant — the passage addresses the drivers' entitlement under the Working Time Regulations and National Minimum Wage Regulations, including the ability to take other driving work during availability time, which is part of the reasoning on worker status and on which working time is compensable. Supports.
[1] Merely notes a Government review of gig-economy protections; it does not answer whether drivers are entitled to NMW/holiday pay. Does not support.
[2] A statement of worker representatives' argument (that waiting time should be paid at the NMW) rather than any determination by the court; it illustrates the controversy but does not help answer the question. Does not support.

uksc/2021/5.rationale: Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5 is the leading and directly on-point authority on whether ride-hailing (app-based) drivers are workers entitled to the national minimum wage and paid annual leave. It is the seminal Supreme Court decision holding that drivers are workers of Uber under contracts to provide services personally, entitled to NMW and holiday pay, and that they are working whenever logged in to the app and able to accept trips. The quoted paragraph 1 states the question in these exact terms, and highlight 2 confirms the Supreme Court's conclusion affirming that drivers qualify for these rights and that working time runs while logged in. Both are directly responsive.

eat/2022/6.rationale: This is a directly on-point EAT authority on the exact question. The claimant, a black-cab driver using the mytaxi app, brought claims for unlawful deduction, failure to pay the national minimum wage and working-time holiday pay, all of which required him to be a "worker" under s.230(3) ERA 1996. The EAT (Lancaster P, Leggatt and Shanks LJJ) dismissed the appeal and upheld the finding that he was a worker, applying Bates van Winkelhof limb (b) ("client or customer" exception) and examining subordination, dependency, control and integration. The judgment is the leading appellate authority cited whenever counsel must advise on whether app-based ride-hailing drivers are workers entitled to NMW and holiday pay, and it discusses the interaction with Uber BV v Aslam / the private-hire licensing regime. Grade 3.

eat/2023/146.rationale: Ryanair DAC v Lutz is not itself a ride-hailing case — it concerns a pilot claiming accrued annual leave under the Civil Aviation (Working Time) Regulations 2004 — but it is a leading EAT authority on limb (b) worker status and on how Uber BV v Aslam is to be applied (written contracts cannot be the starting point; actual working arrangements govern). It therefore substantively assists a lawyer researching whether app-based drivers are entitled to NMW and holiday pay, though it is an application of Uber rather than the direct authority on platform drivers, so 2 rather than 3. The first highlight is tangential (pilot's own leave claim, different sector/regime) but still illustrates the statutory route to accrued annual leave for a limb (b) worker. The second and third are squarely supportive: they identify the very statutory hooks (ERA s 230(3)(b), NMWA s 54(3)(b), WTR reg 2(1)) Uber drivers invoked, and the governing interpretive principle.

eat/2025/32.rationale:
Grade 2. Connaughton is not about ride-hailing drivers, but it is a recent EAT decision squarely concerned with worker status under s.230 ERA, the Working Time Regulations and s.54 NMW 1998, applying Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5 and Autoclenz. Its ratio — that worker status requires a contract of some sort between the parties, and that Uber's 'reality of the relationships' test presupposes such a contractual link — is the reasoning a lawyer would use to situate gig-economy drivers (who always have platform contracts, so the point decided in Connaughton does not exclude them). However, the case concerns GP locums and NHS purchasers, a different factual and subject-matter context, and it neither decides nor analyses Uber drivers' entitlement to NMW or holiday pay; the leading authorities on that remain Aslam itself (grade 3 territory) and Deliveroo/Apex. Useful secondary authority, not directly on point.

Highlights: [0] states the 'contract required' limb of the analysis as applied to a GP with no NHS contract — it frames the boundary of Uber but says nothing about drivers, who necessarily have contracts, so it does not itself answer the question. [1] is supported: it establishes that the NMW Act s.54 and ERA s.230 worker definitions are the same, which is directly transferable to whether the asserted minimum wage and holiday pay rights are statutory rights for workers — the very rights in issue. [2] is supported: it identifies the direct-relationship element found in Uber (and Smith v Cumbers), which is the distinguishing feature relevant to drivers.

uksc/2018/29.rationale: This is the leading and directly on-point Supreme Court authority on exactly the scenario posed: a tradesman (plumber/heating engineer) who was contractually labelled self-employed claiming to be a 'worker' under s.230(3) of the Employment Rights Act in order to bring a discrimination claim under Part 5 of the Equality Act. The judgment settles the modern interpretation (direction/control and subordination, following Allonby, Hashwani and Bates van Winkelhof), holds that labelling in a contract is not determinative, and confirms the tribunal/court approach of treating the three Employment Tribunal decisions as a single composite judgment. It is the first-instance authority any UK lawyer would cite on this question. Of the highlights, only [2] (the policy rationale that self-employed people whose services are largely encompassed within others' businesses should have protection, particularly against discrimination) actually assists in answering the question; [0] is purely factual background about who the parties were and [1] concerns the failed employee-status limb rather than the worker-status route, so neither sheds light on whether the plumber can claim worker status for discrimination purposes.

eat/2025/23.rationale: This is an EAT decision squarely on the issue raised: whether a contractual/labelling arrangement describing someone as a "self-employed independent contractor", and a clause excluding employment, can be determinative of whether that person is in fact a worker (which under the Equality Act 1996 protects against discrimination). The court holds such labels and findings of common intention as to "self-employed" status are not automatically determinative of worker status, because "self-employed"/"independent contractor" are inherently ambiguous terms that may denote either non-employee or non-worker status. The judgment also reviews the third-limb authorities (Byrne Brothers, Cotswold Developments, James v Redcats) and the personal-service/Ready Mixed Concrete line of cases, and remits for proper determination of worker status. That is leading, directly on-point authority for a plumber labelled a self-employed contractor seeking worker status to bring discrimination proceedings. All three highlighted passages go to whether the label/clause is determinative, so each supports the answer.

ewca/civ/2017/51.rationale:
This is the leading Court of Appeal authority on precisely the question posed: whether a tradesperson who was treated and described as self-employed (registered with the Construction Industry Scheme) was nonetheless a 'worker' under s.230(3) ERA limb (b), and an employee for s.83(2)(a) Equality Act 2010 purposes, so as to bring a discrimination claim. The judgment sets out the statutory test, analyses the substitution clause and whether it rendered the plumber a client or customer of his own business, and dismisses the appeal. It is directly on point and squarely answers the query.

On the highlights: [0] states the exact legal issue and holding framework — directly supportive. [1] identifies the claimant as a plumber asserting employment claims, which establishes the factual setting for the 'labelled self-employed' issue — supportive. [2] goes to the crux of the case, i.e. the worker's own belief that he was self-employed and CIS registration supporting that characterisation — supportive. All three aid in answering the question rather than merely sharing vocabulary with it.

eat/2026/109.rationale: This is the very case behind the question. Mathios Berhane v Adebowale & Anor [2026] EAT 109 concerns a tradesman/plumber who was engaged and paid as a self-employed contractor but who needed to establish employee or worker status to bring Equality Act 2010 discrimination claims (and notice pay / unfair dismissal). The EAT's central holding is directly on point: the Employment Tribunal erred in treating the Claimant's status as a self-employed contractor as being in issue, where in fact the Respondents had accepted employee status up to 30 April 2022 and thereafter only worker status on a zero hours contract was in dispute; had the Respondents genuinely asserted self-employment, they would have struck out the Equality Act claims on the basis that those protections do not extend to those running a business. The judgment also addresses the relationship between the notice pay claim (requires employee status) and the discrimination claim (satisfied by worker status), and the distinction between an erroneous belief in self-employment and self-employment in fact. Leading authority on the question posed.

eat/2025/142.rationale: The case is a genuine status-mislabeling dispute: the claimant was contracted and treated by the respondent as a self-employed contractor invoicing through her own limited company (including HMRC IR35 checks, no NHS email requirement, uniform not required, absence from the org chart), while the tribunal found a direct personal contract of employment and treated the written Members Agreement as not reflecting the true relationship. That is substantively the issue raised by a question about someone labelled a self-employed contractor claiming worker status. Two features stop it being squarely on point: the claimant here was a nurse/clinical streamer (not a plumber), and the appeal concerned employment status rather than whether worker status suffices to maintain a discrimination claim — the point of the remittal was to determine status in the first instance. It is therefore useful research (status determined by reality of the working relationship; IR35 tax classification not determinative of employment-law categorisation; section 230(3) ERA 1996 applied) but not a direct authority on the discrimination/jurisdiction aspect. Of the highlights, [0] usefully frames the label-versus-reality conflict, [2] gives the key finding, while [1] merely describes the claimant's other employment and does not advance the question.

ewca/civ/2018/2748.rationale: The question concerns whether a person labelled a self-employed contractor can nonetheless claim "worker" status (for employment/discrimination rights purposes). Uber v Aslam is the leading Court of Appeal authority on precisely that legal issue: it holds that the label the parties (or the platform) impose on the contract does not determine status, and that worker status under s 230(3)(b) ERA 1996 / limb (b) is to be assessed by reference to the statutory and common-law factors (including whether the individual markets himself to the world at large). The facts differ (gig-economy drivers rather than a plumber), but the doctrinal question — contractual self-employment label versus statutory worker status for a discrimination claim — is squarely within Uber's reasoning, which also confirms that the worker definition in the Equality Act 2010 is materially the same. It is therefore a directly on-point and highly persuasive authority for the researcher's question.

eat/2022/6.rationale: The question concerns whether a plumber described as a self-employed contractor nonetheless has limb (b) worker status in order to bring a discrimination claim — i.e. the client-or-customer exception in s.230(3) ERA 1996, and its extension to the Equality Act "employee" definition. Johnson v Transopco is not the plumber's case (it is an Uber driver case) but it is squarely within the same doctrinal framework: it applies Bates van Winkelhof, Windle and Pimlico Plumbers v Smith, and analyses at length when a putative self-employed individual contracting directly with end users is or is not a limb (b) worker, including the point that in some cases "the business is effectively created by the contract" — precisely the plumber-with-no-other-customers problem. It therefore provides substantive, usable guidance for the researcher's question, though it is not the leading or directly on-point authority (Pimlico Plumbers v Smith, Uber BV v Aslam would be), so grade 2 rather than 3.

ewca/civ/2022/12.rationale: This is the leading, directly on-point Court of Appeal authority (13 January 2022) on psychiatric injury to secondary victims who witness a death caused by medical negligence. It consolidated three appeals (Paul, Polmear and Purchase), each concerning relatives who witnessed the traumatic death of a primary victim after the defendant hospital trust's failure to diagnose a life-threatening condition. It settles the core question asked — whether and when proximity exists where the negligently caused death is separated in time from the negligence — holding that the Alcock five elements apply equally to clinical negligence cases and that liability requires the negligence and the horrific event to form a continuum (Walters), with Novo authority barring recovery where the horrific event is a separate event removed in time. This is squarely the authority a lawyer researching the question would cite first, so it merits grade 3 rather than 2: it is not merely useful background but the definitive recent decision on the point. All three highlighted passages help answer the question: highlight 0 defines the scope (liability for psychiatric injury to close relatives of a primary victim in clinical negligence claims); highlight 2 frames the time-interval issue that is the crux of the question; highlight 1 states the operative holding on proximity and the continuum requirement, which is the substantive test a researcher needs.

uksc/2024/1.rationale:
Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust [2024] UKSC 1 is the leading and squarely on-point authority: a claim by close relatives for psychiatric illness caused by witnessing a death resulting from medical negligence (failure to diagnose and treat sepsis leading to death 14.5 months later). The Supreme Court held that the secondary victim claim fell within the Alcock line of exceptional cases, rejecting the "accident"/external traumatic event requirement. The case also reviews and distinguishes Walters, Shorter, Novo and Taylor v Somerset HA, making it indispensable for any research on this question.

Highlight assessment: [0] directly states the holding that an analogous approach applies where medical negligence causes serious illness without death — squarely answers the question. [1] identifies the central issue (whether the death, 14.5 months after the negligence, could be the relevant "event") — directly supports. [2] sets out Chamberlain J's reasoning that the time lag between breach and death is no bar, by reference to analogous authorities — directly supports. All three are genuinely helpful rather than mere keyword overlap.

ewhc/kb/2026/2068.rationale: The question asks for recent cases on psychiatric injury claims by relatives witnessing a death caused by medical negligence. This 2026 EWHC decision is squarely on point: it applies the Supreme Court's decision in Paul (secondary victims in clinical negligence) to strike out the claims of a mother/carer (C2) who alleged psychiatric injury arising from her son (C1)'s death and treatment. Paragraph 116 squarely states the effect of Paul — that a person suffering psychiatric injury from witnessing the death of a close relative from a negligently misdiagnosed medical condition cannot claim as a secondary victim — and paragraph 117 applies that reasoning to hold the other defendants owed no independent direct duty to prevent consequential psychiatric injury to C2. It is therefore a leading, directly on-point recent authority for the question (albeit at the strike-out/summary judgment stage, and while leaving the primary clinical negligence claim struck out for inadequate particulars rather than on the merits). Highlight 0 states the key holding; highlight 1 states the duty analysis as applied. Highlight 2 is a bare procedural ruling that without its subject matter it conveys only the generic strike-out power, so it does not itself answer the question.

ewhc/kb/2026/562.rationale: This is a directly on-point, recent (March 2026) High Court decision on exactly the question asked: whether a relative can claim psychiatric injury where they witness a death or severe injury caused by medical negligence rather than an accident. The judgment analyses Paul and the two conjoined cases, sets out the Leggatt/Lady Rose definition of "accident" for secondary victim claims, identifies why negligently caused "medical crises" fall outside that category, and identifies Walters as the only successful medical negligence secondary victim claim. It is the leading current authority on the boundary of secondary victim recovery in medical negligence deaths, and would be the first case any lawyer researching this question would cite.

ewhc/kb/2024/3480.rationale: This is the High Court judgment (Chamberlain J) reviewing the Supreme Court's decision in Mahmood and Another v Origin Healthcare (UK) Ltd [2024] UKSC 41, which concerned precisely the question asked: whether relatives can recover for psychiatric injury suffered in consequence of witnessing a death (or its immediate aftermath) caused by a doctor's medical negligence. It is a leading, directly on-point authority: it sets out the common law duty of care owed by a doctor to the patient, articulates the "critical question" whether a duty is also owed to close family members to protect them from psychiatric injury, and reviews the secondary victim authorities (Alcock, McLoughlin, Clay, Novo) including temporal proximity and the "first manifestation of damage" points, and whether the rules developed in accident cases extend to medical cases. Directly answers the query and is a recent UKSC/High Court authority of the highest relevance.
